opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about constantly, because "AI lab" and "business" don't always naturally go together. A lot of labs start with the research and figure out the money later, and that can work if you've raised an enormous amount of capital, but for a smaller startup lab you don't really have that luxury.

The way I think about it is that the research has to point toward something people actually need and will pay for. For us, the thing that kept coming up over and over is that data is the bottleneck. Everyone has access to roughly the same models and the same architectures, so what really differentiates you is the quality of the data you train on, evaluate on, and use to specialize models for your own use case. Curating that data well is hard, and most teams don't have the tooling or expertise to do it systematically.

So the business model sort of follows from that. On one side we put out open tools and open research, things like datasets and models that show what's possible when you're careful about data. That builds credibility and community, and it gets people using our tools. On the other side, enterprises come to us when they need help building specialized models or high-quality data pipelines for their domain, and that's where the revenue comes from.

I think the key is not to treat research and product as two separate worlds. The research should de-risk the product, and the product should tell you which research questions actually matter. When those two feed each other, you get a flywheel. When they don't, you either become a consulting shop with no long-term edge, or a research group that runs out of runway.

And the other thing I'd say is to stay focused. It's very tempting in this space to chase every new trend, whether it's agents or reasoning or whatever the hot thing is that month. But as a small lab, you win by going deep on one hard problem that compounds over time, and for us that's data.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprise work and product feedback inform research, but it does not identify design partnerships as a way to learn what the lab should build.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's the question we spent a lot of time on, honestly, because the default answer in this space is "raise a bunch of money, train a model, figure out revenue later," and that's a path that only works if you're one of maybe three or four labs in the world. We're not that, and we didn't want to pretend to be.

So the way I think about it is in layers. At the bottom there's the research, which is where our conviction is. Our bet is that the big general-purpose models are great, but for a lot of real enterprise workloads you don't actually want a giant frontier model. You want something smaller, specialized, that you can run cheaply, that you can fine-tune on your own data, and that behaves predictably. That's an opinion about where value accrues, and it informs everything above it.

The second layer is the product, and this is where we tried to be disciplined. The failure mode for research labs is they build what's intellectually interesting rather than what somebody will pay for. So very early, before we even had a model we were proud of, we went and talked to a lot of companies and asked, what is the thing you're trying to do with LLMs right now that you can't do, or can't do at the cost you need? And the pattern that kept coming up was: we have a prototype on GPT-4 or Claude, it works, but when we try to take it to production the economics don't work, or the latency doesn't work, or we can't send this data out. That's the gap we build for. So the product is really tooling plus models that let a team take that prototype and turn it into something they can actually run at scale.

Then the third layer is how you charge for it, and here I'd say we're still learning. There's the obvious API-style usage pricing, and that's fine, but what we've found is that the companies with the biggest problems want something closer to a partnership. They want you to help them build the specialized model, they want it deployed in their environment, and they're willing to pay for that outcome rather than for tokens. So some of our revenue looks like a platform business and some of it looks more like a services-plus-platform business, and I've made peace with that. I used to think services revenue was a dirty word for a startup. Now I think, early on, it's how you learn what the platform needs to be. The trick is making sure every engagement teaches you something you can productize, so you don't just become a consultancy.

The last thing I'd say is about the lab part specifically. We do publish, we do open-source some things, and people ask how that squares with a business. For us it's pretty simple: it's how we recruit, it's how we build credibility with technical buyers, and it's honestly how we stay sharp. The moat isn't a single model checkpoint, because that depreciates in six months. The moat is the team and the accumulated know-how about how to make smaller models really good at specific things. Being a real research lab is what keeps that compounding. So I don't see the research and the business as being in tension. The business is what lets us keep doing the research, and the research is what makes the business worth anything.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the lab interviewed companies early to learn which production problems to address, and that later customer engagements teach it what to productize. It does not identify those efforts as design partnerships or clearly describe collaborative product design.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the customer problem. What can you help someone do that they couldn’t do before, or that’s currently too expensive or too difficult? And then, where does your research give you a meaningful advantage in solving that problem?

For an AI lab, there’s a tension there. You want enough room to pursue research where the outcome isn’t obvious, but you also need a way to learn whether what you’re building is useful. I’d try to make those two things reinforce each other: work with customers, understand where the technology falls short, and use that to inform the research.

Then the business model depends on how customers get value. An API might make sense in one case; a product that handles an entire workflow might make sense in another. The important thing is that the cost of delivering it—including compute and any human involvement—leaves you with a sustainable business. Technical progress matters, but it has to translate into something people will pay for.

r001.rationale: It recommends working with customers to learn where the technology falls short and using that feedback to inform the research, conveying customer partnerships as a way to guide what the lab builds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to work backward from the value you’re creating for a customer. What’s a problem they care enough about to pay to solve, and why does your research let you solve it better? It’s easy to get excited about a capability, but that alone isn’t a business model.

For an AI lab, there’s also a balance between investing in research that might take time to pay off and finding a product that people need today. I’d look for a tight feedback loop: you put something in customers’ hands, learn where it falls short, and use that to guide the research. Ideally, the research makes the product more valuable, and the revenue lets you keep investing in the research.

r001.rationale: The response recommends putting a product in customers’ hands and learning from feedback, but it does not identify design partnerships as a way to learn what to build.
